issues.issue: This is a recital stating the Depositor 'is the owner of the Trust Fund that is hereby conveyed to the Trustee', which points differently from the operative conveyance mechanics and delivery requirements of Section 2.01 and the acceptance provisions of Section 2.02. In RMBS disputes the question whether and when title actually passed is contested against exactly such recital language.

The provision cites 'Treasury Regulation Section 1.860G-1(a)(4)(ii)' where the parallel REMIC I and REMIC III paragraphs cite subsection (a)(4)(iii), and designates the pool as 'REMIC IT'. These are mechanical/citation slips, though each is readily corrected from the parallel text.

The paragraph headed REMIC III designates the segregated pool as 'REMIC II' and says the Class R-3 Certificates are the residual interests in 'REMIC II', which contradicts its own heading. As a literal matter the designation names the wrong REMIC.

'Accepted Master Servicing Practices' is defined by reference to 'customary mortgage servicing practices of prudent mortgage servicing institutions', an external and unquantified standard whose content is a classic subject of dispute in servicing litigation. Neither 'customary' nor 'prudent' has any benchmark fixed in the Agreement.

The defined term 'Account' is an exhaustive enumeration that omits the Master Servicer Account established by Section 5.01, so provisions using the collective term 'Accounts' may or may not reach that account. The expressio unius inference against an omitted account is arguable.

'Bring Down Agreements' is a closed list of originator purchase and warranty agreements said to be 'assigned to the Trustee', and the scope of what reps were brought down and assigned is precisely what repurchase litigation turns on. Which underlying amended-and-restated agreement governs a given loan is left to inference.

The definition adds Subsequent Recoveries 'pursuant to Section 5.04(b)', but Section 5.04 is the Yield Maintenance Credit Support Annex and Subsequent Recoveries are dealt with under Article VI (Section 6.05). The cross-reference cannot be reconciled with the section it points to.

The definition of the Class A-3 Certificate gives its holder 'the right to the Percentage Interest of distributions provided for the Class A-2 Certificates', naming the wrong class. On its face the mistake gives Class A-3 holders the Class A-2 entitlement.

This definition measures the deduction 'for Realized Losses incurred during the prior calendar month', whereas the parallel Class M-1, M-2, M-3 and M-5 Principal Distribution Amount definitions use 'the related Prepayment Period'. The inconsistent measuring period across otherwise identical formulas cannot be harmonised on the face of the instrument.

The subtraction list in clause (x) skips the Class M-3 Principal Distribution Amount, and clause (b)(2) refers to 'scheduled payments of principal due during the related Prepayment Period' where every parallel definition says Due Period. Both are writing errors that change the computed amount.

The Class P Certificate Account is said to be established 'pursuant to Section 6.09 hereof', but the Agreement has no Section 6.09; the Class P Certificate Account is the subject of Section 6.08. The cross-reference points to a non-existent provision.

The definition designates three different offices for the Securities Administrator and Trustee and separates 'certificate transfer purposes' without an opening clause (i), so which office is the operative address for a given notice or delivery is left unclear. Since notice and delivery obligations run to the 'Corporate Trust Office', the ambiguity has operative consequences.

The Distribution Account is said to be created 'pursuant to Section 5.08', but Article V ends at Section 5.04 and the Distribution Account is established by Section 5.02. The cross-reference points to a section that does not exist.

The closing sentence permits amendment of the rating requirements 'Notwithstanding Section 12.01' and without Certificateholder consent, which sits against the amendment machinery and consent conditions of Section 12.01. Whether the carve-out displaces all of Section 12.01's conditions or only the consent requirement is arguable.

The determination rests on what the Servicer 'in its reasonable good faith judgment, expects to be finally recoverable', a discretionary standard with no objective benchmark, and the Master Servicer's records are 'based solely on information provided by each Servicer'. The point at which a Final Recovery Determination must be made is therefore contestable.

Insurance Proceeds are net of amounts 'released to the Mortgagor in accordance with the procedures that the related Servicer would follow in servicing mortgage loans held for its own account', a self-referential and unverifiable standard. What the Servicer 'would' do for its own account cannot be measured from the instrument.

Master Servicing Compensation is defined as the Master Servicing Fee plus float earnings, but the definition of Master Servicing Fee already includes 'any amounts earned on permitted investments in the Distribution Account during the Master Servicer Float Period'. Read together the two definitions double-count the float, an inconsistency that cannot be harmonised on the face of the text.

The Master Servicing Fee is defined as a rate times Stated Principal Balance 'and any amounts earned on permitted investments in the Distribution Account during the Master Servicer Float Period', yet the separate Master Servicing Compensation definition adds that same float component to the Fee. The overlap makes the compensation actually payable indeterminate.

'Maximum Probable Exposure' is fixed only by 'the EMC's internal risk management process in respect of similar instruments', an undisclosed, unilateral and undefined external standard, and the calculating party is stated twice as the Depositor although the process is EMC's. Neither 'similar instruments' nor the process itself is ascertainable from the Agreement.

The definition of 'MOM Loan' describes MERS acting as mortgagee rather than defining a category of loan, so as written the defined term denotes a person rather than a loan. The mismatch between the term and its definition makes provisions using 'MOM Loan' read oddly.

The definition preserves as a 'Mortgage Loan' any loan not in fact transferred, citing 'a breach of the representation contained in Section 2.03(b)(v) hereof', but Section 2.03(b) is only a survival clause and contains no subsection (v); the loan-level representations sit in the Mortgage Loan Purchase Agreement and Bring Down Agreements. The cross-reference cannot be squared with Section 2.03 as drafted.

The enumerated schedule fields contain duplicated and garbled item letters — two items lettered '(aa)', an item '(¢4)', and 'the the Periodic Rate Cap' — so which data the Schedule must contain is uncertain at those points. The mistakes are mechanical but they affect the content of the operative loan list.

Whether an Advance is 'nonrecoverable' turns entirely on 'the good faith judgment of the Master Servicer or the related Servicer' that it will not be 'ultimately recoverable ... or otherwise', with no objective test or time horizon. Nonrecoverability determinations of this kind are a standing source of dispute between servicers and certificateholders.

After listing named offices the definition adds a catch-all for 'any other officer customarily performing functions similar to those performed by any of the above designated officers', whose reach beyond the enumerated titles is uncertain. The ejusdem generis boundary of that catch-all is not fixed anywhere in the Agreement.

The final proviso excepts 'investments in units of money market funds pursuant to clause (v) above', but clause (v) is guaranteed reinvestment agreements while money market funds are clause (viii). The mis-numbered internal reference leaves the redemption-below-cost carve-out without an identifiable subject.

The 'Prepayment Assumption' is fixed only by reference to a Prospectus Supplement that is not itself part of the Agreement or attached as an exhibit. The operative rate cannot be determined from the four corners of the instrument.

The deduction in clause (ii) subtracts '(b) the Master Servicing Fee Rate' — a per annum rate — from a dollar amount of interest, where the parallel items are fees expressed as amounts. The formula as written cannot be computed literally.

The closing words 'or any replacement policy therefor through the related Interest Accrual Period for such Class relating to a Distribution Date' attach a certificate-class concept to an insurance policy and have no discernible meaning. The sentence as drafted does not parse.

Clause (e) counts Substitution Adjustment Amounts arising from substitution 'pursuant to Section 2.03(d)', but Section 2.03 has no subsection (d); its substitution mechanics are in unlettered paragraphs and the repurchase obligation itself lives in the Mortgage Loan Purchase Agreement. The cross-reference cannot be reconciled with Section 2.03 as written.

'Purchase Price' is defined only for loans required to be repurchased 'pursuant to Section 2.02 hereof' or purchased under Section 4.21, yet Section 2.03 and the definition of 'Mortgage Loans' both require payment of the Purchase Price on repurchases arising under the Mortgage Loan Purchase Agreement and Bring Down Agreements. The definition's stated scope does not cover the repurchases the Agreement elsewhere contemplates.

The clause reads 'reduced by any portion of the Servicing Fee, Servicing Advances and Advances payable to the purchaser of the Mortgage Loan plus and (iii) any costs and damages', with a stray 'plus and' that leaves the relation between the deduction and item (iii) unclear. The predatory-lending damages component is also left at large as 'any costs and damages (if any) incurred by the Trust'.

Requirement (ix) is that a Replacement Mortgage Loan 'comply with each representation and warranty set forth in Section 2.03 hereof', but Section 2.03 contains only the Master Servicer's and Securities Administrator's corporate representations; the loan-level warranties are in the Mortgage Loan Purchase Agreement and Bring Down Agreements. The substitution standard therefore points at the wrong body of representations.

Condition (ii) — 'have a fixed Mortgage Rate not less than or more than 1% per annum higher than the Mortgage Rate of the Deleted Mortgage Loan' — is grammatically incomplete ('not less than' what?) and can be read either as a band around the deleted loan's rate or as a bare ceiling. Condition (iii)'s 'same or higher credit quality characteristics' is equally unmeasured.

The Reserve Fund is said to be created 'pursuant to Section 6.08 hereof', but Section 6.08 is the Class P Certificate Account and the Reserve Fund is created by Section 4.22 ('Reserve Fund; Payments to and from Swap Administrator'). The cross-reference contradicts the section that actually establishes the fund.

The initial $5,000 deposit is said to be made 'pursuant to Section 6.08 hereof', but Section 6.08 is the Class P Certificate Account; the Reserve Fund and its funding are dealt with in Section 4.22. The reference does not match the operative provision.

After naming specific officers the definition sweeps in 'any other officer customarily performing functions similar to those performed by any of the above designated officers', with no boundary on that catch-all. Because trustee duties are triggered by a Responsible Officer's knowledge, whose knowledge counts is a live question.

The last sentence excuses the Servicers from making 'Nonrecoverable Servicing Advances', a capitalised term that appears nowhere else and is not defined in Section 1.01, which defines only 'Nonrecoverable Advance' by reference to Advances. The limit on the advancing obligation therefore has no defined content.

The criteria may be displaced by 'those Servicing Criteria otherwise mutually agreed to ... in response to evolving interpretations of Regulation AB and incorporated into a revised Exhibit N', which leaves the governing standard open-ended. What counts as an 'evolving interpretation' warranting revision is not defined.

The Significance Estimate rests on 'the reasonable good-faith estimate by EMC or its affiliate' of Maximum Probable Exposure, itself defined only by EMC's undisclosed internal risk process. Neither the estimator nor the method can be tested against anything in the Agreement.

The definition runs 'amounts received ... or surplus amounts held ... to cover estimated expenses (including ... recoveries in respect of the representations and warranties made by the Seller ...) specifically related to a Mortgage Loan', so it is unclear whether repurchase-type recoveries on the Seller's warranties are Subsequent Recoveries or merely an example of surplus expense reserves. The syntax leaves the scope of the term genuinely open.

The term is given 'the meaning ascribed to such term pursuant to Section 2.03(d)', but Section 2.03 has no subsection (d); the Substitution Adjustment Amount is defined in an unlettered paragraph of Section 2.03. The pointer does not correspond to the Agreement's own numbering.

'Successor Master Servicer' is said to take its meaning from Section 9.01, which is the Events of Default section, whereas the Agreement's successor master servicer provisions are Sections 8.06 and 9.02 ('Trustee to Act; Appointment of Successor'). The cross-reference does not match the table of contents' allocation of subject matter.

Clause (vi) includes in the Trust Fund 'the rights under the Swap Administration Agreement relating to the Certificates', while the definition of 'Supplemental Interest Trust' states that the Swap Administration Agreement, the Swap Agreement and the related accounts 'do not constitute parts of the Trust Fund or any REMIC'. The two definitions cannot both be right about the same asset.

The allocation adds to more than 100%: 93% to the Class A, M and B Certificates, 3% to the Class CE Certificates and 1% to each of five further classes (Class P, R-1, R-2, R-3 and RX) totals 101%. A voting formula that cannot sum correctly must be construed before any vote can be counted.

This definition attaches the Wells Fargo Assignment Agreement 'as Exhibit R-3', but the definition of the Saxon Assignment Agreement claims the same Exhibit R-3 while the Agreement's exhibit index assigns R-2 to Saxon and R-3 to Wells Fargo. Two different agreements are identified with the same exhibit.

The definition reads 'the cap contract, dated Agreement Provider, including any schedule ...' — the date and the identity of the counterparty have dropped out of the sentence. As written the defining words do not identify the contract at all except by the exhibit reference.

The operative conveyance is of 'all the right, title and interest of the Sellers in and to the assets in the Mortgage Loans', a phrase that does not say whether the Sellers conveyed the loans themselves or only some subset of 'assets in' them. In a transaction whose validity turns on what was conveyed, the wording is materially imprecise.

The delivery list is qualified by three lettered provisos and by phrases such as 'for Mortgage Loans, if the original is not available, a copy' and delivery of a title policy 'within one year of the Closing Date', so what constitutes complete delivery of a Mortgage File is not fixed. Whether the enumerated documents are exhaustive or the provisos excuse them is exactly the kind of question that arises over document defects.

The closing sentence makes the cure/repurchase/substitution obligation 'the sole remedies respecting such defect available to the Certificateholders or to the Securities Administrator on their behalf', omitting the Trustee, who is the party charged with enforcement, and using a singular 'obligation' with plural 'remedies'. Whether this sole-remedy limit binds the Trustee, and what a 'defect in a constituent document' covers, are both open on the words.

The sole-remedy sentence sits against Section 2.02(d), which obliges the Trustee to enforce 'any other obligations of the related Seller or the related Originator under such agreements', and against Section 2.03's independent notice obligation. Read together it is unclear whether remedies beyond repurchase survive.

The Trustee must enforce repurchase 'and any other obligations of the related Seller or the related Originator under such agreements', a general catch-all appended to the specific cure/repurchase/substitute duty whose reach is undefined. What 'any other obligations' the Trustee must enforce, and on what trigger, is left at large.

This enforcement duty is difficult to square with Section 2.02(c), which declares cure, repurchase or substitution to be the 'sole remedies' available in respect of document defects. One provision widens the Trustee's enforcement rights while the other confines them.

The obligation is triggered by 'discovery by any of the parties hereto' of a breach that 'materially and adversely affects the interests of the Certificateholders', and requires 'prompt written notice' — none of 'discovery', 'materially and adversely affects' or 'prompt' is defined. Whether the duty is one of actual discovery or extends to what a party should have known is precisely the sort of question that decides repurchase litigation.

The notice duty runs only to 'the parties hereto', yet the representations whose breach triggers it are those of the Sellers and Originators under the Mortgage Loan Purchase Agreement and Bring Down Agreements, who are not parties to this Agreement, and Section 2.02(d) casts enforcement of those obligations onto the Trustee. Whether a non-party Seller owes any notice obligation cannot be settled from this paragraph alone.

The paragraph directs release of the Mortgage File for 'any Mortgage Loan purchased pursuant to this Section 2.03' and fixes the deposit date by reference to the month in which the Seller 'became obligated to repurchase', but Section 2.03 imposes no repurchase obligation at all — that obligation lives in the Mortgage Loan Purchase Agreement and Bring Down Agreements enforced under Section 2.02(d). The provision presupposes a duty that its own section does not create.

The survival clause says the representations 'set forth in Section 2.03 hereof' survive 'delivery of the respective Mortgage Loans and Mortgage Files to the Trustee', but the only representations in Section 2.03 are the Master Servicer's and Securities Administrator's corporate representations, which have nothing to do with loan delivery. The clause only makes sense if directed at the loan-level warranties in the Mortgage Loan Purchase Agreement and Bring Down Agreements.

The representation is framed in the past tense ('following the transfer ... the Depositor had good title') and is given 'as of the Closing Date', leaving unclear whether title is warranted at the Closing Date or only at some earlier moment. In a trust whose ownership of the loans matters, that timing point is more than stylistic.

The notice trigger reads 'Upon discovery by the Depositor, the Trustee of a breach', with a conjunction missing, so it is unclear whether discovery by either party alone suffices or whether both must discover. The obligation to give 'prompt written notice' is triggered by that very phrase.

The opinion condition applies only to a Mortgage Loan 'that is not in default or as to which default is not reasonably foreseeable', and the deferred repurchase is triggered by 'a default becoming reasonably foreseeable' — a standard with no defined content or decision-maker. Whether default was 'reasonably foreseeable' controls when a repurchase must occur.

The provision requires substitution to satisfy 'the conditions in Section 2.03 and the Mortgage Loan Purchase Agreement or the Bring Down Agreements' and repurchase 'in the same manner as ... pursuant to Section 2.02 or 2.03', although Section 2.03 imposes no repurchase or substitution obligation of its own. The mechanics depend on a section that does not contain them.

Purpose (d) — activities 'necessary, suitable or convenient to accomplish the foregoing or ... incidental thereto or connected therewith' — is a catch-all appended to three specific purposes, and (e) adds 'such other activities as may be required'. How far these general words extend beyond the enumerated purposes is not fixed.

The limitation ends 'while any Certificate is outstanding, and this Section 2.07', a trailing fragment that leaves the sentence without a completed thought. What the closing words add to or subtract from the prohibition cannot be determined.

The Master Servicer's duty is to 'supervise, monitor and oversee' and to act 'in a manner consistent with Accepted Master Servicing Practices', while also having 'full power and authority to do any and all things which it may deem necessary or desirable'. The combination of an external customary-practice standard with unfettered discretion leaves the content of the duty contestable.

Enforcement must be carried out 'to such an extent and at such time as the Master Servicer ... in its good faith business judgment, would require were it the owner of the related Mortgage Loans', a hypothetical-owner standard with no objective measure. The final sentence's escape — no Trustee obligation to assume duties 'unless the Trustee has not been able to find a successor servicer' — is equally open-ended.

The bond and policy need only be 'in such form and amount generally acceptable for entities serving as master servicers or trustees', a market-practice standard with no stated amount, deductible or measuring date. Whether any given coverage satisfies it cannot be answered from the Agreement.

The paragraph provides for release against 'a request for release signed by a Servicing Officer', then imposes obligations by reference to 'Such trust receipt', a document the provision never mentions or requires. The instrument that fixes the return obligation is therefore unidentified.

The access sentence — 'The Master Servicer, the related Servicer shall provide access to information and documentation regarding the Mortgage Loans to the Trustee and, regarding the Mortgage Loans and their respective agents and accountants' — is ungrammatical and it cannot be told who must give access to whom. The duplicated 'regarding the Mortgage Loans' clause destroys the sense of the obligation.

Insurance collections are said to be deposited 'Pursuant to Sections 5.01 and 5.04' and to be subject to withdrawal 'pursuant to Sections 5.02, 5.03 or 5.04', but Section 5.04 is the Yield Maintenance Credit Support Annex and has nothing to do with insurance proceeds. The account mechanics point at a section that does not supply them.

The Master Servicer must use 'its best reasonable efforts' to keep primary mortgage insurance in force, a hybrid of two different efforts standards that is not defined anywhere in the Agreement. Whether 'best reasonable efforts' means best efforts or merely reasonable efforts is a genuine question.

The provision routes insurance collections 'Pursuant to Sections 5.01 and 5.05', but Article V of this Agreement ends at Section 5.04 and contains no Section 5.05. The deposit mechanism cites a provision that does not exist.

Foreclosure is required only for loans 'as to which no satisfactory arrangements can be made for collection of delinquent payments', with no indication of who judges satisfactoriness or by what measure. The trigger for realization is therefore left to argument.

This section awards the Master Servicing Fee and, separately, 'all income and gain realized from any investment of funds in the Distribution Account ... during the Master Servicer Float Period', whereas the Section 1.01 definitions of 'Master Servicing Fee' and 'Master Servicing Compensation' already fold that float income into the Fee. The three provisions cannot all be given effect without paying the float twice.

The proviso allows early reimbursement of 'any such unreimbursed Monthly Advances', but the Agreement defines 'Advance' and 'Servicing Advances' and nowhere uses or defines 'Monthly Advances'. The class of advances that may be recovered from rental income is therefore not identified by any defined term.

This paragraph deems any failure to comply with Section 4.16 an 'Event of Default' and declares that it 'shall supersede any other provision in this Agreement or any other agreement to the contrary', which cuts across the definition of Event of Default ('As defined in Section 9.01') and the notice, cure and successor machinery of Article IX. Whether a reporting lapse terminates the Master Servicer without the Article IX process cannot be resolved without construing both.

The paragraph makes any non-compliance with Section 4.17 an 'Event of Default' and states that it 'shall supersede any other provision in this Agreement or any other agreement to the contrary', which sits against the Section 9.01 definition of Events of Default and the Article IX termination procedure. The two termination routes for the Master Servicer cannot both stand unqualified.

The deadlines cross over: the Master Servicer must sign the Form 8-K 'no later than the close of business ... on the 3rd Business Day after the Reportable Event' while the Depositor's approval or changes are due 'no later than the close of business on the 3rd Business Day after the Reportable Event', so signature can be required before the document is approved. Which deadline yields is not stated.

Item (IV) requires 'a Sarbanes-Oxley Certification as described in Section 4.18(a)(ii)(D) below', but the Sarbanes-Oxley Certification is prescribed in Section 4.18(a)(iii)(D); subsection (a)(ii) deals with Form 8-K. The Form 10-K content requirement points to the wrong subsection.

The opening sentence collapses — 'Additional Form 10-D Disclosure, Additional Form 10- Disclosure or any Form 8-K Disclosure Information (collectively, the obligation to include such Additional Information ... is subject to receipt' — so the collective defined term is never closed, and the paragraph then obliges 'The Master Servicer, the Seller, the Securities Administrator and the Depositor' to notify and provide information to those same four parties. Neither the defined term nor the direction of the obligation can be read off the text.

Section 1.01 defines 'Additional Disclosure' as 'As defined in Section 4.18', yet the broken parenthetical in this paragraph never completes that definition. The defined term relied on throughout Section 4.18 has no source.

Contribution is to be made 'in such proportion as is appropriate to reflect the relative fault and the relative benefit of the respective parties', with no method, decision-maker or tie-breaker between fault and benefit. The measure of contribution is left entirely at large.

The paragraph deems non-compliance with Section 4.18 an 'Event of Default' permitting immediate termination and declares that it 'shall supersede any other provision in this Agreement or any other agreement to the contrary', which cannot be squared with the Section 9.01 definition of Events of Default and the Article IX notice and successor procedure. It also directs the reader to 'this Section 4.18(d)' for the termination, although subsection (d) is the email-delivery provision.

This subsection permits amendment of Section 4.18 'Notwithstanding the provisions of Section 12.01' and without Certificateholder consent, cutting across the Agreement's general amendment provision and its consent protections. How much of Section 12.01 is displaced — consent only, or also its other conditions such as rating-agency or opinion requirements — is not said.

Clause (b) requires obligations to be 'supplemented and modified as necessary' to conform to 'interpretive advice or guidance, convention or consensus among active participants in the asset-backed securities markets, advice of counsel, or otherwise', a standard whose content is indeterminate and which no party is identified to fix. The obligations of the parties can shift without any ascertainable trigger.

Clause (d) provides that 'no amendment of this Agreement shall be required' to change the parties' obligations to accommodate evolving Regulation AB interpretations, which conflicts with the amendment machinery of Section 12.01 governing how this Agreement's terms may be changed. One provision permits obligations to change without amendment while the other prescribes how amendments must be made.

The obligation to file financing statements is imposed on 'the Seller', but the Sellers (EMC and the Sponsor) are not parties to this Agreement, whose parties are the Depositor, Wells Fargo and Deutsche Bank. The section purports to bind someone the opening paragraph of the Agreement does not make a party.

The purchase option is conferred on 'Saxon or the Majority Class CE Certificateholder', yet the last sentence says 'This right may be assigned by the Seller to a third party' — the Seller is not the holder of the right. The reinstatement sentence also makes the option exercisable 'as of the first day of the related Fiscal Quarter' although the option is otherwise not tied to Fiscal Quarters.

The Swap Account is created and maintained by the Swap Administrator under the Swap Administration Agreement and is held in the Supplemental Interest Trust, yet this subsection makes investment turn on 'written instructions to the Securities Administrator' and has the Securities Administrator remit swap receipts. Which of the Swap Administrator, the Supplemental Interest Trust Trustee and the Securities Administrator controls the account is not consistently stated.

This subsection establishes and funds the Reserve Fund, but the Section 1.01 definitions of 'Reserve Fund' and 'Reserve Fund Deposit' say the account is created and the deposit made 'pursuant to Section 6.08 hereof'. The Agreement therefore identifies two different sections as the source of the same account.
